title: Deliver real-time AI experiences with Azure Web PubSub

questions.q: An on-call developer, an incident commander and a database specialist must all watch the same AI investigation update live. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Azure Web PubSub with an operation group
options.why: Correct. One worker publish reaches every authorized connection in the group.

options.text: An SSE stream tied to the developer's request
options.why: SSE from one request doesn't fan out to others by itself.

options.text: Polling every 60 seconds
options.why: Polling is for infrequent changes and multiplies requests.

options.text: Direct HTTP streaming to the first requester
options.why: The stream is tied to one request; others need a relay.

questions.hint: Several people, independently connected, all watching the same thing.
questions.explain: Choose Web PubSub when independent recipients or group delivery justify it.

questions.q: Which content type does a Server-Sent Events response use?

options.text: application/cloudevents+json
options.why: That's for publishing CloudEvents to Event Grid.

options.text: text/event-stream
options.why: Correct. SSE uses a long-lived text/event-stream response.

options.text: multipart/form-data
options.why: That's form uploads.

options.text: application/json
options.why: That's ordinary JSON.

questions.hint: SSE responses have their own MIME type.
questions.explain: SSE adds event data, names and IDs on top of a long-lived HTTP response.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An assistant streams a log summary to the browser with SSE.

rows.text: The browser's EventSource normally tries to reconnect after an interruption.
After reconnecting, missed events are replayed even if the server never stored them.
rows.why: The server needs retained events and resume logic.

rows.text: Approving a finding should go through a separate authenticated HTTP request.
rows.why: SSE is one-way; commands use HTTP.

rows.text: SSE lets the browser send approvals back on the same event stream.
rows.why: SSE is one-way; commands go through separate HTTP requests.

questions.hint: EventSource reconnects by itself, but replay depends on what the server kept.
questions.explain: SSE is one-way with reconnection; resume depends on retained events.

questions.q: An existing app uses Azure SignalR Service hubs and client method invocation. A developer proposes swapping in the Web PubSub client library. What does Learn say?

options.text: Web PubSub clients are drop-in replacements for SignalR clients
options.why: Learn says not to assume this.

options.text: Switch to polling first, then to Web PubSub
options.why: Polling isn't a migration step for this.

options.text: SignalR is required for every WebSocket application
options.why: Web PubSub suits WebSocket apps with their own contract.

options.text: Evaluate SignalR integration; it isn't drop-in
options.why: Correct. SignalR has its own programming model (hubs, method invocation).

questions.hint: SignalR and Web PubSub are related, but their programming models differ.
questions.explain: SignalR and Web PubSub are related but distinct services.

questions.q: An archived-log analysis takes several minutes and only ever shows three states: queued, processing and completed. One user watches it. Which delivery approach does Learn suggest evaluating first?

options.text: A WebSocket that the browser holds open for the whole analysis
options.why: A live channel adds complexity that three state changes don't justify.

options.text: Periodic status requests against a status endpoint
options.why: Correct. Infrequent background status changes can be served by polling, without a live messaging channel.

options.text: Azure Web PubSub with a group per user
options.why: Web PubSub fits many independent recipients or group delivery, which this scenario doesn't need.

options.text: Azure SignalR Service hubs
options.why: SignalR is for hub-based app models, which isn't needed for three status updates.

questions.hint: Start with the simplest option that meets the experience you need.
questions.explain: Begin with the client experience. For a single generated answer, evaluate HTTP streaming or SSE; for infrequent background status, evaluate polling; choose Web PubSub for independently connected recipients, group delivery or connection scale.

questions.q: A FastAPI endpoint streams a generated answer with SSE, and locally the text appears word by word. In production, behind a reverse proxy, the whole answer appears at once at the end. What's the likely cause?

options.text: The model sends the whole answer at once in production
options.why: It streams locally with the same model, which points to buffering along the way.

options.text: A proxy, compression layer or framework is buffering the response
options.why: Correct. Verify incremental delivery through the actual hosting stack, because layers in between can buffer.

options.text: The browser's EventSource waits for the connection to close
options.why: EventSource processes events as they arrive when nothing buffers them.

options.text: SSE only works over HTTP/1.0
options.why: That isn't the issue. The response is being held back somewhere between the app and the browser.

questions.hint: It works locally. What sits between the app and the browser in production?
questions.explain: An HTTP stream isn't automatically visible as soon as the backend writes a chunk: a reverse proxy, compression layer or framework can buffer it. Verify incremental delivery through the real hosting stack.

questions.q: A developer proposes publishing new investigation requests to a Web PubSub group so that "a worker picks them up". What's wrong?

options.text: Web PubSub can't carry JSON payloads to clients
options.why: Web PubSub carries JSON envelopes.

options.text: Groups can hold at most one connection each
options.why: Groups collect many connections; the issue is broadcast vs reliable assignment.

options.text: Groups broadcast; they don't assign work to one worker
options.why: Correct. Use a queue or workflow for backend processing.

options.text: Groups require Durable Functions to work at all
options.why: Web PubSub doesn't require Durable Functions.

questions.hint: A group delivers to everyone in it. It doesn't hand one job to one worker.
questions.explain: A group isn't a Service Bus subscription or competing-consumer queue.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A worker stores a completed report, then crashes before publishing the completion notification.

rows.text: Connected browsers might keep showing older progress.
Clients can recover the completed result through the status endpoint.
The AI operation must be repeated to send the notification.
rows.why: Recovery via status avoids repeating the AI work.

rows.text: A Web PubSub group publish and the database write commit as one atomic transaction.
rows.why: A database write and a Web PubSub publish aren't one atomic transaction.

questions.hint: The durable record is the truth. A missed notification doesn't undo completed work.
questions.explain: Persist first; use an outbox when eventual notification is required.

questions.q: A responder closes the browser tab during an investigation. What should happen to the backend work?

options.text: It's cancelled automatically when the connection drops
options.why: Disconnecting isn't a cancellation.

options.text: It continues; cancelling is a separate command
options.why: Correct. Lost connections don't cancel work; cancellation is a deliberate command.

options.text: It pauses until any responder reconnects
options.why: Work doesn't depend on a connected browser.

options.text: It's marked failed because delivery failed
options.why: Delivery problems don't turn successful processing into failure.

questions.hint: Closing a tab isn't a decision to stop the investigation.
questions.explain: Separate processing outcomes from delivery problems.

questions.q: A worker updates the operation record in the database and must eventually publish a matching Web PubSub notification, even if it crashes right after the database write. Which pattern fits?

options.text: Publish the notification first, then write to the database
options.why: Clients could then see "completed" before the result exists.

options.text: A transactional outbox: store the notification with the state change, and let a publisher send pending ones
options.why: Correct. Recording the notification in the same transaction means a separate publisher can send it later.

options.text: Ask each browser to reconnect every minute
options.why: Reconnecting doesn't produce the missing notification. Clients would need to read the status API.

options.text: Rely on Web PubSub to retry the notification after the crash
options.why: Web PubSub can't send something the crashed worker never published.

questions.hint: Put the notification somewhere durable, in the same transaction as the state change.
questions.explain: Persist state before notifying. When eventual publishing is required, record the notification with the state change in a transactional outbox; a separate publisher sends pending notifications and marks them sent.

questions.q: A browser should only observe updates for one investigation. Which role should its Web PubSub token include?

options.text: Web PubSub Service Owner
options.why: That's an Azure RBAC role for backend identities.

options.text: `webpubsub.joinLeaveGroup.<that-group>`
options.why: Correct. It permits joining and leaving that one group, not publishing.

options.text: `webpubsub.joinLeaveGroup` (unrestricted)
options.why: Unrestricted join lets it join any group.

options.text: `webpubsub.sendToGroup`
options.why: That lets the client publish to groups.

questions.hint: Observers need to join one group and nothing more.
questions.explain: Grant the smallest group-scoped role for receive-only clients.

questions.q: The negotiation endpoint receives userId and groupName in the request body from the browser. What should the backend do?

options.text: Derive identity and group on the server
options.why: Correct. Browser-supplied IDs and group names aren't identity assertions.

options.text: Copy them into the token after URL-encoding them
options.why: Encoding doesn't authorize anything.

options.text: Use the values if they contain no forward slashes
options.why: Format checks don't establish authorization.

options.text: Trust the values, since the user is already signed in
options.why: Signed-in status doesn't make client fields trustworthy.

questions.hint: Never trust what the browser says about who it is.
questions.explain: Authorize the operation, then derive user ID and group on the server.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A backend uses its managed identity with Microsoft Entra ID to generate client tokens.

rows.text: The identity needs the generateToken action and clientConnection/write.
Web PubSub Service Owner includes both permissions but grants broader access.
rows.why: A custom role can be narrower.

rows.text: Developer role assignments automatically apply to the deployed managed identity.
rows.why: Assign deployed identities their own roles.

questions.hint: Token generation needs two permissions. Developer role assignments don't carry over.
questions.explain: Backend Azure permissions and client token roles are separate boundaries.

questions.q: A responder is removed from an incident while their browser tab is still connected. What should the backend do?

options.text: Deny negotiation, revoke permission, remove from group
options.why: Correct. Expiry doesn't revoke active connections; act on each tracked connection.

options.text: Send a message asking the browser to leave the group
options.why: The browser isn't trusted to enforce access.

options.text: Nothing; the client token will expire on its own soon
options.why: Expiry only blocks new connections.

options.text: Rotate the Web PubSub access key for the service
options.why: Key rotation doesn't target this user's connection.

questions.hint: Removing access means stopping future connections and cutting off the current one.
questions.explain: Track connection IDs; use revoke_permission() and remove_connection_from_group().

questions.q: An operation group's name must not expose tenant or operation IDs, and IDs may contain delimiter characters. How does Learn suggest naming the group?

options.text: Join the tenant and operation IDs with a hyphen
options.why: Delimiters inside IDs could collide, and the IDs would be exposed.

options.text: Use the signed-in user's email address
options.why: That exposes personal data and scopes the group to the user, not to the operation.

options.text: Hash an unambiguous encoding of the tenant and operation IDs into a stable, opaque name
options.why: Correct. This avoids collisions from delimiters and keeps IDs out of routing names.

options.text: Let the browser choose a random group name and send it to the backend
options.why: Browser-supplied group names aren't trusted.

questions.hint: You want a name that's stable, collision-free, and reveals nothing.
questions.explain: Derive a stable, opaque group name by hashing an unambiguous encoding of tenant and operation IDs. That avoids collisions from delimiters and avoids exposing IDs in routing names.

questions.q: Which Python client callback type delivers messages that a service publishes to a group?

options.text: CallbackType.GROUP_MESSAGE
options.why: Correct. Group broadcasts arrive through GROUP_MESSAGE.

options.text: CallbackType.CONNECTED
options.why: CONNECTED reports connection, not messages.

options.text: CallbackType.SERVER_MESSAGE
options.why: SERVER_MESSAGE is for messages sent directly to a connection or user.

options.text: CallbackType.REJOIN_GROUP_FAILED
options.why: That reports a failed rejoin.

questions.hint: The callback type is named after where the message was sent.
questions.explain: Route group notifications through validated handlers under a lock.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A worker publishes notification `op42-event-15` with sequence 15.

rows.text: If the publish is retried, it should reuse event ID op42-event-15 and sequence 15.
rows.why: One logical update keeps its IDs across retries.

rows.text: A successful send_to_group() proves every responder saw the update.
rows.why: Publish success doesn't prove browser processing or human receipt.

rows.text: The final text batch alone shows the operation succeeded.
rows.why: Wait for operation.completed; validation or persistence can still fail.

questions.hint: Retries keep the same identity. Sending isn't proof of reading. Notifications don't replace durable state.
questions.explain: Persist, then publish with stable IDs; completion is its own event.

questions.q: Generated findings arrive as Markdown and the browser renders them as HTML. What does Learn require?

options.text: Strip the sequence numbers before rendering
options.why: Sequences are needed for ordering, and aren't the issue.

options.text: Render raw HTML for richer formatting
options.why: Raw HTML risks script injection.

options.text: Trust it because it came from your own model
options.why: Model output is untrusted.

options.text: Render as text; sanitize Markdown-to-HTML
options.why: Correct. Model output isn't trusted browser markup.

questions.hint: Generated text is untrusted, so render it safely.
questions.explain: Validate payloads before mutating view state.

questions.q: The browser has applied updates through sequence 15 and receives sequence 17. What should it do?

options.text: Hold 17 and fetch current operation state
options.why: Correct. A gap means a missed update; reconcile with a snapshot.

options.text: Close the connection and reload the whole page
options.why: Reloading isn't the recovery step Learn describes.

options.text: Apply 17 and continue with the stream
options.why: Applying out of order can corrupt generated text.

options.text: Ignore 17 because it's a duplicate
options.why: Duplicates have the same or lower sequence.

questions.hint: Sequence 16 is missing. Don't apply 17 on top of a gap.
questions.explain: Duplicate → ignore; next → apply; gap → hold and fetch state.

questions.q: Put Learn's recovery flow for an operation in order.
steps: Register handlers and mark the view unsynchronized
Connect and wait for operation-group membership
Buffer notifications while requesting the status snapshot
Replace the view with the snapshot and set last_sequence to its watermark
Discard buffered events at or below the watermark and apply newer ones
questions.hint: Mark the view unsynchronized, connect and join, buffer, then rebuild from the snapshot.
questions.explain: Subscribing before requesting the snapshot avoids losing updates in between.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A browser reconnects with a brand-new connection after the reliable session couldn't be recovered.

rows.text: It needs fresh negotiation and its group membership restored.
rows.why: New connections reauthorize and restore membership.

rows.text: auto_rejoin_groups also recreates memberships the server assigned to the old connection.
rows.why: It tracks only groups joined by client code.

rows.text: A snapshot whose lastSequence is lower than what the view shows should replace the view.
rows.why: Don't replace newer output with an older snapshot.

rows.text: If completion was the last event and was missed, no later gap will reveal it.
rows.why: Reconcile after reconnects and inactivity, not only on gaps.

questions.hint: A new connection means new negotiation, and server-assigned groups don't come back by themselves.
questions.explain: Recovery = reauthorize, restore membership, reconcile durable state.

questions.q: A batcher only checks elapsed time when a new token arrives, and during model pauses short batches sit unsent. What fixes this?

options.text: Lower the item threshold to a single fragment
options.why: One-item batches defeat batching.

options.text: Publish every model token immediately instead
options.why: Per-token publishing adds overhead and fan-out traffic.

options.text: Flush on a timer, not only on new fragments
options.why: Correct. Time-based flushing must not depend on the next fragment arriving.

options.text: Increase the batch size budget for each batch
options.why: Larger batches make the delay worse.

questions.hint: A batch that waits for the next token never flushes during a pause.
questions.explain: Flush on time, count, size or operation boundary.

questions.q: Match each update type to Learn's overflow policy.
choices: Preserve order, or restore from durable state
Persist and keep discoverable via status

items.why: A newer snapshot replaces older ones.

questions.hint: Some updates can be replaced by newer ones. Others must never be dropped.
questions.explain: Define which updates can be coalesced before choosing an overflow policy.

questions.q: During heavy load, a worker can't keep up with publishing a progress snapshot for every log file it scans. Which overflow policy does Learn give for progress snapshots?

options.text: Persist every snapshot and keep each one discoverable
options.why: That policy is for approval requests and terminal outcomes.

options.text: Preserve every snapshot in order
options.why: Strict order is for generated-text deltas, which can't be skipped.

options.text: Keep only the newest snapshot and drop older pending ones
options.why: Correct. A newer snapshot replaces older progress, so older ones can be dropped.

options.text: Block the AI work until every snapshot is delivered
options.why: Slowing the work for progress messages isn't the policy Learn gives.

questions.hint: Which kind of update makes the previous one useless?
questions.explain: Overflow policies differ by update type: progress snapshots keep only the newest; generated-text deltas preserve order or restore from durable state; approval requests and terminal outcomes are persisted and stay discoverable via status.
